# Chapter 18 The Stieltjes Integral

In this chapter we discuss a generalization of the Riemann integral that is often used in both theoretical and applied mathematics. Stieltjes<sup>1</sup> originally introduced this concept to deal with infinite continued fractions,<sup>2</sup> but it was soon apparent that the concept is useful in other areas of mathematics—and thus in mathematical physics, probability, and number theory, independently of its role in continued fractions. We illustrate the usefulness of the concept with two simple examples. 

Example 18.1. Consider a planar curve parameterized by $\gamma ( t ) = { \bigl ( } x ( t ) , y ( t ) { \bigr ) } \ ( t \in$ $[ a , b ] )$  , where the x-coordinate function is strictly monotone increasing and continuous, and the y-coordinate function is nonnegative on $[ a , b ]$ . The problem is to find the area under the region bounded by the curve. If $a = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n } = b$ is a partition of the interval $[ a , b ]$ and $c _ { i } \in [ t _ { i - 1 } , t _ { i } ]$ for all i, then the area can be approximated by the sum 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} y (c _ {i}) \big (x (t _ {i}) - x (t _ {i - 1}) \big).
$$

We can expect the area to be the limit—in a suitable sense—of these sums. 

Example 18.2. Consider a metal rod of negligible thickness but not negligible mass $M > 0$ . Suppose that the rod lies on the interval $[ a , b ]$ , and let the mass of the rod over the subinterval $[ a , x ]$ be $m ( x )$ for all $x \in [ a , b ]$ . Our task is to find the center of mass of the rod. 

We know that if we place weights $m _ { 1 } , \ldots , m _ { n }$ at the points $x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n }$ , then the center of mass of this system of points $\{ x _ { 1 } , \ldots , x _ { n } \}$ is 

$$
\frac {m _ {1} x _ {1} + \cdots + m _ {n} x _ {n}}{m _ {1} + \cdots + m _ {n}}.
$$

Consider a partition $a = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n } = b$ and choose points $c _ { i } \in [ t _ { i - 1 } , t _ { i } ]$ for all i. If we suppose that the mass distribution of the rod is continuous (meaning that the mass of the rod at every single point is zero), then the mass of the rod over the interval $\left[ t _ { i - 1 } , t _ { i } \right]$ is $m ( t _ { i } ) - m ( t _ { i - 1 } )$ . Concentrating this weight at the point $c _ { i }$ , the center of mass of the system of points $\{ c _ { 1 } , \ldots , c _ { n } \}$ is 

$$
\frac {c _ {1} \left(m (t _ {1}) - m (t _ {0})\right) + \cdots + c _ {n} \left(m (t _ {n}) - m (t _ {n - 1})\right)}{M}.
$$

This approximates the center of mass of the rod itself, and once again, we expect that the limit of these numbers in a suitable sense will be the center of mass. 

We can see that in both examples, a sum appears that depends on two functions. In these sums, we multiply the value of the first function (which, in Example 18.2, was the function x) at the inner points by the increments of the second function. 

We use the following notation and naming conventions. Let $f , g \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ be given functions, let $F \colon a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots < x _ { n } = b$ be a partition of the interval $[ a , b ]$ and let $c _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right] ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ be arbitrary inner points. Then the sum 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f (c _ {i}) \cdot \left(g (x _ {i}) - g (x _ {i - 1})\right)
$$

is denoted by $\sigma _ { F } \left( f , g ; \left( c _ { i } \right) \right)$ , and is called the approximating sum of $f$ with respect to $g .$ . 

Definition 18.3. Let $f , g \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ be given functions. We say that the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ off with respect to g exists and has value I if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that if $F \colon a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots < x _ { n } = b$ is a partition of $[ a , b ]$ with mesh smaller than $\delta$ and $c _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right] ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ are arbitrary inner points, then 

$$
\left| \sigma_ {F} (f, g; (c _ {i})) - I \right| <   \varepsilon .\tag{18.1}
$$

Remarks 18.4. 1. Let $g ( x ) = x$ for all $x \in [ a , b ]$ . It is clear that the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists exactly when the Riemann integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f$ dx does, and in this case, their 'values agree. 

2. If the function $g$ is constant, then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ always exists, and its value is zero. If the function $f$ 'is constant and has value c, then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ always exists and has value $c \cdot { \bigl ( } g ( b ) - g ( a ) { \bigr ) }$ 

3. The existence of the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ is not guaranteed by f and g being Riemann integrable in $[ a , b ]$ '. One can show that if f and g share a point of discontinuity, then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ does not exist. (See Exercise 18.4.) Thus if $f$ and $g$ 'are bounded functions in $[ a , b ]$ and are continuous everywhere except at a common point, then they are both Riemann integrable in $[ a , b ]$ , while the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ does not exist. 

4. For the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ to exist, it is not even sufficient for $f$ and $g$ to be continuous in $[ a , b ]$ '. See Exercise 18.5. 

Now we show that if $g$ is strictly monotone and continuous, then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ can be reduced to a Riemann integral. 

Theorem 18.5. $\begin{array} { r } { { I f g \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R } } } \end{array}$ is strictly monotone increasing and continuous, then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists ifand only ifthe Riemann integral $\textstyle \int _ { g ( a ) } ^ { g ( b ) } f \circ g ^ { - 1 }$ dx does, and then 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} f d g = \int_ {g (a)} ^ {g (b)} f \circ g ^ {- 1} d x.
$$

Proof. If $F \colon a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots < x _ { n } = b$ is a partition and $c _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right] ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ are arbitrary inner points, then the points $t _ { i } = g ( x _ { i } ) ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ give us a partition $\overline { F }$ of the interval $[ g ( a ) , g ( b ) ]$ ], and we have $g ( c _ { i } ) \in [ g ( x _ { i - 1 } ) , g ( x _ { i } ) ]$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n .$ Then 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f \left(c _ {i}\right) \cdot \left(g \left(x _ {i}\right) - g \left(x _ {i - 1}\right)\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left(f \circ g ^ {- 1}\right) \left(g \left(c _ {i}\right)\right) \cdot \left(t _ {i} - t _ {i - 1}\right)\tag{18.2}
$$

is an approximating sum of the Riemann sum $\textstyle \int _ { g ( a ) } ^ { g ( b ) } f \circ g ^ { - 1 } d x$ . Conversely, if we have $\overline { { F } } \colon g ( a ) = t _ { 0 } < t _ { 1 } < \cdots < t _ { n } = g ( b )$ as a partition of the interval $[ g ( a ) , g ( b ) ]$ and $d _ { i } \in [ t _ { i - 1 } , t _ { i } ]$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n ,$ , then the points $x _ { i } = g ^ { - 1 } ( t _ { i } ) ( i = 1 , \dots , n )$ create a partition $F$ of the interval $[ a , b ]$ . If $c _ { i } = g ^ { - 1 } ( d _ { i } )$ , then $c _ { i } \in [ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } ]$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n .$ and (18.2) holds. 

By the uniform continuity of $g ,$ , we know that for every $\delta > 0 .$ , if the partition F has small enough mesh, then $\overline { F }$ has mesh smaller than $\delta .$ . Thus comparing statement (iii) of Theorem 14.23 with equality (18.2), we get that if the Riemann integral $\boldsymbol { \int _ { g ( a ) } ^ { g ( b ) } f \circ g ^ { - 1 } }$ dx exists, then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ also exists, and they are equal. 

Since the function $g ^ { - 1 }$ is also uniformly continuous, it follows that for every $\delta > 0$ , if the partition $\overline { F }$ has small enough mesh, then $F$ has mesh smaller than $\delta$ Thus by the definition of the Stieltjes integral, by statement (iii) of Theorem 14.23, and by equality (18.2), it follows that if the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists, then the Riemann integral $\textstyle \int _ { g ( a ) } ^ { g ( b ) } f \circ g ^ { - 1 }$ dx exists as well, and they have the same value. 

The following statements can be deduced easily from the definition of the Stieltjes integral. We leave their proofs to the reader. 

## Theorem 18.6.

(i) If the Stieltjes integrals $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f _ { 1 } d g$ and $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f _ { 2 } d g$ exist, then for all $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R }$ the Stieltjes integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { b } ( c _ { 1 } f _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } f _ { 2 } ) d g } \end{array}$ exists as well, taking on the value $c _ { 1 } \cdot \textstyle { \int _ { a } ^ { b } f _ { 1 } d g + c _ { 2 } \cdot \int _ { a } ^ { b } f _ { 2 } d g }$ 

(ii) If the Stieltjes integrals $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g _ { 1 }$ and $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g _ { 2 }$ exist, then for all $c _ { 1 } , c _ { 2 } \in \mathbb { R }$ , the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d ( c _ { 1 } g _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } g _ { 2 } )$ exists as well, and has value $\textstyle c _ { 1 } \cdot \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g _ { 1 } +$ $c _ { 2 } \cdot \textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g _ { 2 }$ 

The following theorem gives us a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of Stieltjes integrals. For the proof of the theorem, see Exercise 18.6. 

Theorem 18.7 (Cauchy’s Criterion). The Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists if and only iffor every $\varepsilon > 0 ,$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that if $F _ { 1 }$ 'and $F _ { 2 }$ are partitions $o f [ a , b ]$ with mesh smaller than $\delta ,$ then 

$$
\left| \sigma_ {F _ {1}} (f, g; (c _ {i})) - \sigma_ {F _ {2}} (f, g; (d _ {j})) \right| <   \varepsilon
$$

with an arbitrary choice ofthe inner points $c _ { i }$ and $d _ { j }$ . 

With the help of Cauchy’s criterion, it is easy to prove the following theorem. We leave the proof to the reader once again. 

Theorem 18.8. If the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists, then for all $a < c < b ,$ , the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { c } f d g$ and $\textstyle \int _ { c } ^ { b } f d g$ also exist, and $\textstyle { \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g = \int _ { a } ^ { c } f d g + \int _ { c } ^ { b } f d g . }$ 

We should note that the existence of the Stieltjes integrals $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { c } f d g$ and $\textstyle \int _ { c } ^ { b } f d g$ alone does not imply the existence of $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ (see Exercise 18.2). If, however, at least one of $f$ and $g$ is continuous at $^ { c , }$ 'and the other function is bounded then the existence of $\textstyle { \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g }$ already follows (see Exercise 18.3). 

'The following important theorem shows that the roles of f and $g$ in the Stieltjes integral are symmetric in some sense. We remind our readers that $[ F ] _ { a } ^ { b }$ denotes the difference $F ( b ) - F ( a )$ 

Theorem 18.9 (Integration by Parts). If the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists, then $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } g d f$ also exists, and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g + \int _ { a } ^ { b } g d f = [ f \cdot g ] _ { a } ^ { b } . } \end{array}$ 

Proof. The proof relies on Abel’s rearrangement (see equation (14.31)). 

Let $F \colon a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots < x _ { n } = b$ be a partition, and let $c _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right] \ ( i =$ $1 , \ldots , n )$ be inner points. If we apply Abel’s rearrangement to the approximating sum σ $\left( g , f ; \left( c _ { i } \right) \right)$ , we get that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sigma_ {F} (g, f; (c _ {i})) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} g (c _ {i}) \cdot (f (x _ {i}) - f (x _ {i - 1})) = \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad = f (b) g (b) - f (a) g (a) - \sum_ {i = 0} ^ {n} f (x _ {i}) (g (c _ {i + 1}) - g (c _ {i})), \end{array}\tag{18.3}
$$

where $c _ { 0 } = a$ and $c _ { n + 1 } = b$ . Since $a = c _ { 0 } \leq c _ { 1 } \leq \ldots \leq c _ { n + 1 } = b$ and $x _ { i } \in \left[ c _ { i } , c _ { i + 1 } \right]$ for all $i = 0 , \ldots , n .$ , we have 

$$
\sum_ {i = 0} ^ {n} f (x _ {i}) \big (g (c _ {i + 1}) - g (c _ {i}) \big) = \sigma_ {F ^ {\prime}} \big (f, g; (d _ {i}) \big),\tag{18.4}
$$

where $F ^ { \prime }$ denotes the partition defined by the points $c _ { i } \ ( 0 \leq i \leq n )$ with the corresponding inner points. (We list each of the $c _ { i }$ points only once. Note that on the lefthand side of (18.4), we can leave out the terms in which $c _ { i } = c _ { i + 1 } . )$ Then by (18.3), 

$$
\sigma_ {F} (g, f; (c _ {i})) = [ f \cdot g ] _ {a} ^ {b} - \sigma_ {F ^ {\prime}} (f, g; (d _ {i})).
$$

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given, and suppose that $\delta > 0$ satisfies the condition of Definition 18.3. It is easy to see that if the mesh of the partition F is smaller than $\delta / 2$ , then the mesh of $F ^ { \prime }$ is smaller than $\delta ,$ and so $\left| \sigma _ { F ^ { \prime } } \mathopen { } \mathclose \bgroup \left( f , g ; ( d _ { i } ) \aftergroup \egroup \right) - I \right| < \varepsilon$ , where $\textstyle I = \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ . This shows that if the mesh of $F$  <sub>is smaller than</sub> $\delta / 2$ , then $\left| \sigma _ { F } \left( g , f ; ( c _ { i } ) \right) - \left( [ f g ] _ { a } ^ { b } - I \right) \right| <$ for an arbitrary choice of the inner points. It follows that the integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } g d f$ exists, and that its value is $[ f g ] _ { a } ^ { b } - I$ □ 

Since Cauchy’s criterion (Theorem 18.7) is hard to apply in deciding whether a specific Stieltjes integral exists, we need other conditions guaranteeing the existence of the Stieltjes integral that can be easier to check. The simplest such condition is the following. 

Theorem 18.10. Ifone ofthefunctions f and g defined on the interval $[ a , b ]$ is continuous, while the other is of bounded variation, then the Stieltjes integrals $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ and $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } g d f$ exist. 

Proof. By Theorem 18.9, it suffices to prove the existence of the integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ and we can also assume that $f$ is continuous and $g$ 'is of bounded variation. By Theorems 17.8 and 18.6, it suffices to consider the case that $g$ is monotone increasing. 

For an arbitrary partition F : $a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots < x _ { n } = b$ , let 

$$
s _ {F} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} m _ {i} \cdot (g (x _ {i}) - g (x _ {i - 1})) \quad \text { and } \quad S _ {F} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} M _ {i} \cdot (g (x _ {i}) - g (x _ {i - 1})),
$$

where $m _ { i } = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ f ( x ) \colon x \in [ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } ] \}$ and $M _ { i } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ f ( x ) \colon x \in [ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } ] \}$ for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n .$ . Since $g ( x _ { i } ) - g ( x _ { i - 1 } ) \geq 0$ for all i, 

$$
s _ {F} \leq \sigma_ {F} (f, g; (c _ {i})) \leq S _ {F}\tag{18.5}
$$

with any choice of inner points $c _ { i }$ . 

It is easy to see that $s _ { F _ { 1 } } \leq S _ { F _ { 2 } }$ for any partitions $F _ { 1 }$ and $F _ { 2 }$ (by repeating the proofs of Lemmas 14.3 and 14.4, using that $g$ is monotone increasing). Thus the set of “lower $\mathrm { s u m s } ^ { \prime \prime } \ : s _ { F }$ is nonempty and bounded from above. If I denotes the supremum of this set, then $s _ { F } \leq I \leq S _ { F }$ for every partition $F$ 

Now we show that $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists, and its value is I. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. By 'Heine’s theorem, f is uniformly continuous on $[ a , b ]$ , so there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that $| f ( x ) - f ( y ) | < \varepsilon$ whenever $x , y \in [ a , b ]$ and $\vert x - y \vert < \delta$ . Let $F \colon a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots <$ $x _ { n } = b$ be an arbitrary partition with mesh smaller than $\delta$ . By Weierstrass’s theorem, for each i, there are points $c _ { i } , d _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right]$ such that $f ( c _ { i } ) = m _ { i }$ and $f ( d _ { i } ) = M _ { i }$ . Then $\vert d _ { i } - c _ { i } \vert \leq x _ { i } - x _ { i - 1 } < \delta$ , so by our choice of $\delta .$ , we have $M _ { i } - m _ { i } = f ( d _ { i } ) - f ( c _ { i } ) < \varepsilon$ Thus 

$$
\begin{array}{l} S _ {F} - s _ {F} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (M _ {i} - m _ {i}) \cdot \big (g (x _ {i}) - g (x _ {i - 1}) \big) \leq \varepsilon \cdot \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \big (g (x _ {i}) - g (x _ {i - 1}) \big) = \\ \qquad = \big (g (b) - g (a) \big) \cdot \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Now using (18.5), we get that 

$$
I - (g (b) - g (a)) \cdot \varepsilon <   s _ {F} \leq \sigma_ {F} (f, g; (c _ {i})) \leq S _ {F} <   I + (g (b) - g (a)) \cdot \varepsilon
$$

for arbitrary inner points $c _ { i } .$ . This shows that $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists and that its value is I. 

Remark $I 8 . I I .$ . One can show that the class of continuous functions and the class of functions of bounded variation are “dual classes” in the sense that a function f is continuous if and only if $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists for all functions g that are of bounded variation, and a function g is of bounded variation if and only if $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists for every continuous function $f .$ (See Exercises 18.8 and 18.9.) 

The following theorem can often be applied to computing Stieltjes integrals. 

Theorem 18.12. If f is Riemann integrable, g is differentiable, and $g ^ { \prime }$ is Riemann integrable on $[ a , b ]$ , then the Stieltjes integral off with respect to g exists, and 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b} f d g = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f \cdot g ^ {\prime} d x.\tag{18.6}
$$

Proof. Since f and $g ^ { \prime }$ are integrable on $[ a , b ]$ , the Riemann integral on the righthand side of (18.6) exists. Let its value be I. We want to show that for an arbitrary $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that for every partition $a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots < x _ { n } = b$ with mesh smaller than δ, (18.1) holds with an arbitrary choice of inner values $c _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right] ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ 

Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. Since f is Riemann integrable on $[ a , b ]$ , there must exist a $\delta _ { \mathrm { l } } > 0$ such that $\Omega _ { F } ( f ) < \varepsilon$ whenever the partition $F$ has mesh smaller than $\delta _ { 1 }$ By Theorem 14.23, there exists a $\delta _ { 2 } > 0$ such that whenever $a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots <$ $x _ { n } = b$ is a partition with mesh smaller than $\delta _ { 2 }$ 

$$
\left| I - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f (d _ {i}) g ^ {\prime} (d _ {i}) (x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1}) \right| <   \varepsilon\tag{18.7}
$$

holds for arbitrary inner points $d _ { i } \in [ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } ] ( i = 1 , \dots , n )$ 

Let $\delta = \operatorname* { m i n } ( \delta _ { 1 } , \delta _ { 2 } )$ , and consider an arbitrary partition $F \colon a = x _ { 0 } < x _ { 1 } < \cdots <$ $x _ { n } = b$ with mesh smaller than δ. Let $c _ { i } \in \left[ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } \right] ( i = 1 , \ldots , n )$ be arbitrary inner points. 

Since $g$ is differentiable on $[ a , b ]$ , by the mean value theorem, 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f \left(c _ {i}\right) \left(g \left(x _ {i}\right) - g \left(x _ {i - 1}\right)\right) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f \left(c _ {i}\right) g ^ {\prime} \left(d _ {i}\right) \left(x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1}\right)\tag{18.8}
$$

for suitable numbers $d _ { i } \in [ x _ { i - 1 } , x _ { i } ]$ . Let K denote an upper bound of $| g ^ { \prime } |$ on $[ a , b ]$ Then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| I - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f (c _ {i}) \big (g (x _ {i}) - g (x _ {i - 1}) \big) \right| = \left| I - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f (c _ {i}) g ^ {\prime} (d _ {i}) (x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1}) \right| \leq \\ \leq \left| I - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} f (d _ {i}) g ^ {\prime} (d _ {i}) (x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1}) \right| + \left| \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \big (f (c _ {i}) - f (d _ {i}) \big) g ^ {\prime} (d _ {i}) (x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1}) \right| <   \\ <   \varepsilon + K \cdot \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \omega (f; [ x _ {i - 1}, x _ {i} ]) \cdot (x _ {i} - x _ {i - 1}) = \varepsilon + K \cdot \Omega_ {F} (f) <   (1 + K) \cdot \varepsilon , \end{array}
$$

which concludes the proof of the theorem. 

Remarks 18.13. 1. The conditions for the existence of the integral in Theorem 18.12 can be significantly weakened. So for example, the integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ is guaranteed to exist if $f$ is Riemann integrable and $g$ 'is Lipschitz (see Exercise 18.11). 

2. In the statement above, the Lipschitz property of $g$ can be weakened further. We say that the function $f \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ is absolutely continuous if for each $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that whenever $[ a _ { 1 } , b _ { 1 } ] , \ldots , [ a _ { n } , b _ { n } ]$ are nonoverlapping subintervals of $[ a , b ]$ such that $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \left( b _ { i } - a _ { i } \right) < \delta$ , then $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } | f ( b _ { i } ) - f ( a _ { i } ) | < \varepsilon$ . One can show that if f is Riemann integrable and g is absolutely continuous in $[ a , b ]$ , then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists. 

'3. The class of Riemann integrable functions and the class of absolutely continuous functions are also dual: a function f is Riemann integrable if and only if $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists for every absolutely continuous function $^ { g , }$ and a function $g$ 'is absolutely continuous ifand only if $\dot { \int _ { a } ^ { b } } f d g$ existsfor every Riemann integrablefunction $f .$ . The 'proof of this theorem, however, uses concepts from measure theory that we do not deal with in this book. 

A number-theoretic application. In the introduction of the chapter we mentioned that Stieltjes integrals pop up in many areas of mathematics, such as in number theory. Dealing with an important problem—namely the distribution of the prime numbers—we often need to approximate sums that consist of the values of specific functions at the prime numbers. For example, $\begin{array} { r } { L ( x ) = \sum _ { p \leq x } ( \log p ) / p } \end{array}$ and $\textstyle R ( x ) = \sum _ { p < x } 1 / p$ are such sums. In these sums, we need to add the numbers $( \log p ) / p$ or $1 / p$ for all prime numbers $p$ less than or equal to x. Transforming these sums (often using Abel’s rearrangement) can be efficiently done with the help of the Stieltjes integral, as shown by the following theorem. 

Let a sequence $a _ { 1 } < a _ { 2 } < \cdots$ that tends to infinity and the function $\varphi$ defined at the numbers $a _ { n }$ be given. Let $\begin{array} { r } { A ( x ) = \sum _ { a _ { n } \leq x } \varphi ( a _ { n } ) } \end{array}$ . (If $\left( a _ { n } \right)$ is the sequence of prime numbers and $\varphi ( x ) = ( \log x ) / x$ , then $A ( x ) = L ( x )$ , and if $\varphi ( x ) = 1 / x .$ , then $A ( x ) = R ( x ) . )$ 

Theorem 18.14. Suppose that f is differentiable and f is integrable on $[ a , b ]$ , where $a < a _ { 1 } \leq b .$ . Then 

$$
\sum_ {a _ {n} \leq b} f (a _ {n}) \cdot \varphi (a _ {n}) = f (b) \cdot A (b) - \int_ {a} ^ {b} A (x) \cdot f ^ {\prime} (x) d x.\tag{18.9}
$$

Proof. We show that $\textstyle \sum _ { a _ { n } \leq b } f ( a _ { n } ) \cdot \varphi ( a _ { n } ) = \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d A$ . The function $A ( x )$ is constant on the interval $\left[ a _ { n - 1 } , a _ { n } \right)$ ', and has a jump discontinuity at the point $a _ { n }$ , and there, $A ( a _ { n } ) - \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to a _ { n } - 0 } A ( x ) = \varphi ( a _ { n } )$ . Thus if we take a partition of the interval $[ a , b ]$ with mesh small enough, then any approximating sum of the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d A$ will 'consist of mostly zero terms, except for the terms that correspond to a subinterval containing one of $a _ { n } \leq b$ , and the nth such term will be close to $f ( a _ { n } ) \cdot \varphi ( a _ { n } )$ by the continuity of $f .$ 

Now integration by parts (Theorem 18.9) gives 

$$
\sum_ {a _ {n} \leq b} f (a _ {n}) \cdot \varphi (a _ {n}) = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f d A = f (b) \cdot A (b) - \int_ {a} ^ {b} A d f = f (b) \cdot A (b) - \int_ {a} ^ {b} A \cdot f ^ {\prime} d x,
$$

also using Theorem 18.12. 

If $\left( a _ { n } \right)$ is the sequence of prime numbers and $\varphi \equiv 1$ , then the value of $A ( x )$ is the sum of prime numbers up to x, that is $\pi ( x )$ . This gives us the following corollary. 

Corollary 18.15. Suppose that f is differentiable and f is integrable on the interval $[ 1 , x ] \ ( x \geq 2 )$ . Then 

$$
\sum_ {p \leq x} f (p) = f (x) \cdot \pi (x) - \int_ {1} ^ {x} \pi (t) \cdot f ^ {\prime} (t) d t.\tag{18.10}
$$

If, for example, $f ( x ) = 1 / x .$ , then we get that $\textstyle \sum _ { p \leq x } 1 / p \geq \int _ { 2 } ^ { x } ( \pi ( t ) / t ^ { 2 } ) d t$ . Now there exists a constant $c > 0$ such that $\pi ( x ) \geq c \cdot x { \bar { / } }$ 'logx. (See [5], Corollary 8.6.) Since $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { e } ^ { x } d t / ( t \cdot \log t ) = \log \log x . } \end{array}$ , we get that $\Sigma _ { p \leq x } 1 / p \geq c$ loglogx. This proves the 'following theorem. 

Corollary 18.16. 

$$
\sum_ {p} \frac {1}{p} = \infty .
$$

We can get a much better approximation for the partial sums if we use the fact that the difference between the function $\begin{array} { r } { L ( x ) = \sum _ { p \leq x } ( \log p ) / p } \end{array}$ and logx is bounded. (A proof of this fact can be found in [5, Theorem 8.8(b)].) Let $\eta \left( x \right) = L ( x ) - \log x .$ 

Let $\left( a _ { n } \right)$ be the sequence of prime numbers, and apply (18.9) with the choices $\varphi ( x ) = ( \log x ) / x$ and $f ( x ) = 1 / \log x .$ Then $A ( x ) = L ( x )$ , and so 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \sum_ {p \leq x} \frac {1}{p} = \frac {L (x)}{\log x} + \int_ {2} ^ {x} \frac {L (t)}{t \cdot \log^ {2} t} d t = \\ \qquad = 1 + \frac {\eta (x)}{\log x} + \int_ {2} ^ {x} \frac {1}{t \cdot \log t} d t + \int_ {2} ^ {x} \frac {\eta (t)}{t \cdot \log^ {2} t} d t = \\ \qquad = \log \log x - \log \log 2 + 1 + \frac {\eta (x)}{\log x} + \int_ {2} ^ {x} \frac {\eta (t)}{t \cdot \log^ {2} t} d t. \end{array}
$$

Here if $x \to \infty$ , then $\eta ( x ) / \log x$ tends to zero, and we can also show that the integral $\begin{array} { r l } { \int _ { 2 } ^ { x } \left( \eta ( t ) / ( t \cdot \log ^ { 2 } t ) \right) } \end{array}$ dt has a finite limit as $x \to \infty ;$ this follows easily by the theory of '  improper integrals; see the next chapter. Comparing all of this, we get the following. 

Theorem 18.17. The limit lim $\begin{array} { r } { \mathfrak { l } _ { X  \infty } ( \sum _ { p \leq x } \frac { 1 } { p } - \log \log x ) } \end{array}$ exists and is finite.

18.10. Let $\mathcal { F }$ be an arbitrary set of functions defined on the interval $[ a , b ]$ . Let $\mathcal { G }$ be the set of those functions $g \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ for which the integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists for all $f \in \mathcal F$ . Furthermore, let $\mathcal { H }$ denote the set of functions $h \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ whose integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } h d g$ exists for all $g \in { \mathcal { G } }$ . Show that $\mathcal { H }$ and $\mathcal { G }$ are dual classes, that is, a function h satisfies $h \in \mathcal { H }$ if and only if $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } h d g$ exists for all $g \in { \mathcal { G } }$ , and a function g satisfies $g \in { \mathcal { G } }$ if and only if $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } h d g$ exists for all $h \in \mathcal { H }$ 

18.11. Prove that if f is Riemann integrable and g is Lipschitz on $[ a , b ]$ , then the Stieltjes integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d g$ exists. (H) 

## 18.12. Show that

(a) if f is Lipschitz, then it is absolutely continuous; 

(b) if f is absolutely continuous, then it is continuous and of bounded variation. 

# Chapter 19 The Improper Integral

## 19.1 The Definition and Computation of Improper Integrals

Until now, we have dealt only with integrals of functions that are defined in some closed and bounded interval (except, perhaps, for finitely many points of the interval) and are bounded on that interval. These restrictions are sometimes too strict; there are problems whose solutions require us to integrate functions on unbounded intervals, or that themselves might not be bounded. 

Suppose that we want to compute the integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \pi / 2 } { \sqrt { 1 + \sin x } } d x$ with the substitution sin $x = t$ . The formulas x = arcsint, $d x / d t = 1 / \sqrt { 1 - t ^ { 2 } }$ give 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\pi / 2} \sqrt {1 + \sin x} d x = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \frac {\sqrt {1 + t}}{\sqrt {1 - t ^ {2}}} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \sqrt {\frac {1}{1 - t}} d t.\tag{19.1}
$$

The integral on the right-hand side, however, is undefined (for now), since the function $\sqrt { 1 / ( 1 - t ) }$ is unbounded, and so it is not integrable in $[ 0 , 1 ]$ ]. (This problem is caused by the application of the substitution formula, Theorem 15.21, with the choices $f ( x ) = { \sqrt { 1 + \sin x } } .$ $g ( t ) = \arcsin t$ $[ a , b ] = [ 0 , 1 ]$ . The theorem cannot be , applied, since its conditions are not satisfied, the function arcsint not being differentiable at 1.) 

Wanting to compute the integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \pi } d x / ( 1 + \sin x )$ with the substitution $\scriptstyle \mathbf { t g } ( x / 2 ) = t$ ', we run into trouble with the limits of integration. Since $\mathrm { l i m } _ { x  \pi - 0 }$ $\mathfrak { t g } ( x / 2 ) = \infty$ , the result of the substitution is 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\pi} \frac {1}{1 + \sin x} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \frac {1}{1 + 2 t / (1 + t ^ {2})} \cdot \frac {2}{1 + t ^ {2}} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} 2 \cdot \frac {d t}{(1 + t) ^ {2}},\tag{19.2}
$$

and the integral on the right-hand side is undefined (for now). (Here the problem is caused by the function $\mathrm { t g } ( x / 2 )$ not being defined—and so not being differentiable— at π.) 

We know that if the function $f \colon [ a , b ]  \mathbb { R }$ is differentiable and $f ^ { \prime }$ is integrable on $[ a , b ]$ , then the graph of $f$ is rectifiable, and its arc length is $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { b } \sqrt { 1 + ( f ^ { \prime } ( x ) ) ^ { 2 } d x } } \end{array}$ '(see Theorem 16.13 and Remark 16.21). We can expect this equation to give us the arc length of the graph of $f$ whenever the graph is rectifiable and $f$ is differentiable with the exception of finitely many points. This, however, is not always so. Consider, for example, the function $f ( x ) = { \sqrt { x } }$ on $[ 0 , 1 ]$ . Since $f$ is monotone, its graph is rectifiable. On the other hand, $f$ is differentiable at every point $x > 0$ , and 

$$
\sqrt {1 + (f ^ {\prime} (x)) ^ {2}} = \sqrt {1 + \frac {1}{4 x}}.
$$

We expect the arc length of $\sqrt { x }$ over $[ 0 , 1 ]$ to be 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} \sqrt {1 + \frac {1}{4 x}} d x.\tag{19.3}
$$

However, this integral is not defined (for now), because the function we are integrating is not bounded. 

We can avoid all of these problems by extending the concept of the integral. 

Definition 19.1. Let f be defined on the interval $[ a , \infty )$ , and suppose that $f$ is integrable on $[ a , b ]$ for all $b > a ,$ . If the limit 

$$
\lim _ {b \to \infty} \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x = I
$$

exists and is finite, then we say that the improper integral of $f$ in $[ a , \infty )$ is convergent and has value I. We denote this by $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \infty } f ( x ) d x = I$ 

If the limit li $\scriptstyle \mathtt { n } _ { b \to \infty } \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x )$ '<sub>dx does not exist or exists but is not finite, then we say</sub> 'that the improper integral is divergent. If 

$$
\lim _ {b \to \infty} \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x = \infty \quad (\text { or } - \infty),
$$

then we say that the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x )$ dx exists, and its value is $\infty \left( \mathrm { o r } - \infty \right)$ We define the improper integral $\int _ { - \infty } ^ { a } { \ddot { f } } ( x )$ dx similarly. 

Example 19.2. By the definition above, the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } d x / ( 1 + x ) ^ { 2 }$ is convergent, and its value is 1. Indeed, the function $1 { \dot { / } } ( 1 + x ) ^ { \frac { } { 2 } }$ 'is integrable on the interval $[ 0 , b ]$ for all $b > 0$ , and 

$$
\lim _ {b \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {0} ^ {b} \frac {d x}{(1 + x) ^ {2}} = \lim _ {b \rightarrow \infty} \left[ - \frac {1}{(1 + x)} \right] _ {0} ^ {b} = \lim _ {b \rightarrow \infty} \left[ 1 - \frac {1}{(1 + b)} \right] = 1.
$$

Once we know this, it is easy to see that equality (19.2) truly holds, and the value of the integral on the left is 2. Indeed, for all $0 < b < \pi$ , the function $\mathrm { t g } ( x / 2 )$ is differentiable, and its derivative is integrable on $[ 0 , b ]$ , so the substitution $\mathbf { t g } ( x / 2 ) = t$ can be used here. Thus 

19.1 The Definition and Computation of Improper Integrals 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {b} \frac {d x}{1 + \sin x} = \int_ {0} ^ {\operatorname{tg} (b / 2)} \frac {1}{1 + 2 t / (1 + t ^ {2})} \cdot \frac {2}{1 + t ^ {2}} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {\operatorname{tg} (b / 2)} 2 \cdot \frac {d t}{(1 + t) ^ {2}}.
$$

Now using the theorems regarding the continuity of the integral function (Theorem 15.5) and regarding the limit of compositions of functions, we get that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {\pi} \frac {d x}{1 + \sin x} = \lim _ {b \to \pi - 0} \int_ {0} ^ {b} \frac {d x}{1 + \sin x} = \\ = \lim _ {b \to \pi - 0} \int_ {0} ^ {\operatorname{tg} (b / 2)} 2 \cdot \frac {d t}{(1 + t) ^ {2}} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} 2 \cdot \frac {d t}{(1 + t) ^ {2}} = 2. \end{array}
$$

We define the integrals appearing in the right-hand side of (19.1) and those in (19.3) in a similar way. 

Definition 19.3. Let $[ a , b ]$ be a bounded interval, let f be defined on $[ a , b )$ , and suppose that $f$ is integrable on the interval $[ a , c ]$ for all $a \leq c < b$ . If the limit 

$$
\lim _ {c \rightarrow b - 0} \int_ {a} ^ {c} f (x) d x = I
$$

exists and is finite, then we say that the improper integral of the function f is convergent and its value is I. We denote this by $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x ) d x = I .$ 

If the limit $\textstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { c \to b - 0 } \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x )$ dx does not exist, or exists but is not finite, then we 'say that the improper integral is divergent. If 

$$
\lim _ {c \to b - 0} \int_ {a} ^ {c} f (x) d x = \infty (\mathrm{or} - \infty),
$$

then we say that the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x )$ dx exists, and that its value is ∞ $( \mathrm { o r } - \infty )$ 

We define the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x )$ dx similarly in the case that $f$ is integrable on the intervals $[ c , b ]$ for all $a < c \leq b$ 

Remarks 19.4. 1. We say that an improper integral exists if it is convergent or if its value is ∞ or ∞. (In these last two cases, the improper integral exists but is divergent.) 

2. If f is integrable on the bounded interval $[ a , b ]$ , then the expression $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f ( x )$ dx now 'denotes three numbers at once: the Riemann integral of the function f over the interval $[ a , b ]$ , the limit $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { c \to b - 0 } \int _ { a } ^ { c } f ( x ) d x . } \end{array}$ and the limit $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { c \to a + 0 } \int _ { c } ^ { b } } \end{array}$ $f ( x ) d x$ ' '. Luckily, these three numbers agree; by Theorem 15.5, the integral function $\textstyle I ( x ) = \int _ { a } ^ { x } f ( t )$ dt is continuous on $[ a , b ]$ , so 

$$
\lim _ {c \rightarrow b - 0} \int_ {a} ^ {c} f (x) d x = \lim _ {c \rightarrow b - 0} I (c) = I (b) = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x,
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {c \rightarrow a + 0} \int_ {c} ^ {b} f (x) d x = \lim _ {c \rightarrow a + 0} [ I (b) - I (c) ] = I (b) - I (a) = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f (x) d x.
$$

In other words, if the Riemann integral of the function f exists on the interval $[ a , b ]$ then (both of) its improper integrals exist there, and their values agree with those of the Riemann integral. Thus the concept of the improper integral is an extension of the Riemann integral. 

Even though this is true, when we say that f is integrable on the closed interval $[ a , b ]$ , we will still mean that f is Riemann integrable on $[ a , b ]$ 

Example 19.5. The integral on the right-hand side of equality (19.1) is convergent, and its value is 2. Clearly, we have 

$$
\lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \int_ {0} ^ {c} \sqrt {\frac {1}{1 - t}} d t = \lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \left[ - 2 \sqrt {1 - t} \right] _ {0} ^ {c} = \lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} (2 - 2 \sqrt {1 - c}) = 2.
$$

Using the argument of Example 19.2, we can easily check that equality (19.1) is true. 

Now for some further examples.

$$
\int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {d x}{x ^ {c}} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 1 / (c - 1), & \text { if } c > 1, \\ \infty , & \text { if } c \leq 1. \end{array} \right.\tag{19.4}
$$

For $c \neq 1$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {d x}{x ^ {c}} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {d x}{x ^ {c}} =\\\qquad = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} \left[ \frac {1}{1 - c} \cdot x ^ {1 - c} \right] _ {1} ^ {\omega} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} \left[ \frac {1}{c - 1} + \frac {1}{1 - c} \cdot \omega^ {1 - c} \right].\end{array}
$$

Now 

$$
\lim _ {x \to \infty} x ^ {1 - c} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text { if } c > 1, \\ \infty , & \text { if } c <   1, \end{array} \right.

so if $c \neq 1$ , then (19.4) is true. On the other hand, 

$$
\int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {d x}{x} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {d x}{x} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} [ \log x ] _ {1} ^ {\omega} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} \log \omega = \infty ,
$$

so (19.4) also holds when $c = 1$

For $c \neq 1$ , we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l}\int_ {0} ^ {1} \frac {d x}{x ^ {c}} = \lim _ {\delta \rightarrow 0 + 0} \int_ {\delta} ^ {1} \frac {d x}{x ^ {c}} =\\\qquad = \lim _ {\delta \rightarrow 0 + 0} \left[ \frac {1}{1 - c} \cdot x ^ {1 - c} \right] _ {\delta} ^ {1} = \lim _ {\delta \rightarrow 0 + 0} \left[ \frac {1}{1 - c} - \frac {1}{1 - c} \cdot \delta^ {1 - c} \right]\end{array}

for all $0 < \delta < 1$ . Now

\lim _ {x \to 0 + 0} x ^ {1 - c} = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text { if } c <   1, \\ \infty , & \text { if } c > 1, \end{array} \right.

so if $c \neq 1$ , then (19.5) is true. On the other hand,

\int_ {\delta} ^ {1} \frac {d x}{x} = \lim _ {\delta \rightarrow 0 + 0} [ \log x ] _ {\delta} ^ {1} = \lim _ {\delta \rightarrow 0 + 0} [ - \log \delta ] = \infty ,

so (19.5) also holds when $c = 1$ (Figure 19.1). 

Incidentally, the substitution $x = 1 / t$ gives us that

$$

This shows that statements (19.4) and (19.5) follow each from the other. (We will justify this statement soon, in Theorem 19.12.)

\begin{array}{c} \int_ {2} ^ {\infty} \frac {d x}{x \cdot \log^ {c} x} = \lim _ {\omega \to \infty} \int_ {2} ^ {\omega} \frac {d x}{x \cdot \log^ {c} x} = \lim _ {\omega \to \infty} \left[ \frac {1}{1 - c} \cdot \log^ {1 - c} x \right] _ {2} ^ {\omega} = \\ = \lim _ {\omega \to \infty} \left[ \frac {1}{c - 1} \cdot \log^ {1 - c} 2 + \frac {1}{1 - c} \cdot \log^ {1 - c} \omega \right]. \end{array}
$$

Now

\lim _ {x \to \infty} \log^ {1 - c} x = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} 0, & \text { if } c > 1, \\ \infty , & \text { if } c <   1, \end{array} \right.

so if $c > 1$ , then the integral is convergent, while if $c < 1$ , then it is divergent. In the case $c = 1$ ,

\begin{array}{c}\int_ {2} ^ {\infty} \frac {d x}{x \cdot \log x} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {2} ^ {\omega} \frac {d x}{x \cdot \log x} = \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} [ \log \log x ] _ {2} ^ {\omega} =\\= \lim _ {\omega \rightarrow \infty} [ \log \log \omega - \log \log 2 ] = \infty ,\end{array}
$$

so the integral is also divergent when $c = 1$

$$

5. $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } d x / ( 1 + x ^ { 2 } ) = \pi / 2$ , since $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega  \infty } \int _ { 0 } ^ { \omega } d x / ( 1 + x ^ { 2 } ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega  \infty } [ \mathrm { a r c } \mathrm { t g } x ] _ { 0 } ^ { \omega } = } \end{array}$ $\pi / 2$ . We can similarly see that $\textstyle \int _ { - \infty } ^ { 0 } d x / ( 1 + x ^ { 2 } ) = \pi / 2$

\begin{array}{c} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \log x d x = \lim _ {\delta \to 0 + 0} \int_ {\delta} ^ {1} \log x d x = \lim _ {\delta \to 0 + 0} [ x \log x - x ] _ {\delta} ^ {1} = \\ = \lim _ {\delta \to 0 + 0} [ - \delta \log \delta + \delta - 1 ] = - 1. \end{array}
$$

7. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } d x / ( 1 - x ^ { 2 } )$ is divergent, since

\lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \int_ {0} ^ {c} \frac {d x}{1 - x ^ {2}} = \lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \left[ \frac {1}{2} \cdot \log \left| \frac {1 + x}{1 - x} \right|\right] _ {0} ^ {c} = \lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \left[ \frac {1}{2} \cdot \log \left| \frac {1 + c}{1 - c} \right|\right] = \infty .
$$

8. $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } d x / \left( { \sqrt { 1 - x ^ { 2 } } } \right) = \pi / 2$ , since

\lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \int_ {0} ^ {c} \frac {d x}{\sqrt {1 - x ^ {2}}} = \lim _ {c \rightarrow 1 - 0} \operatorname{arc} \sin c = \frac {\pi}{2}.
$$

We sometimes need to compute integrals that are “improper” at both endpoints, and possibly at numerous interior points as well. The integrals $\textstyle \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } } d x ,$ $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } { \sqrt { x } } \cdot e ^ { - x } d x$ , and $\textstyle { \int _ { - 1 } ^ { 1 } d x } / { \sqrt { | x | } }$ are examples of this. We define these in the follow-'ing way. 

Definition 19.6. Let the function f be defined on the finite or infinite interval $( \alpha , \beta )$ except at at most finitely many points. Suppose that there exists a partition $\alpha = c _ { 0 } <$ $c _ { 1 } < \cdots < c _ { n - 1 } < c _ { n } = \beta$ with the property that for all $i = 1 , \ldots , n .$ , the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { c _ { i - 1 } } ^ { c _ { i } } f ( x )$ dx is convergent by Definition 19.1 or by Definition 19.3. Then we say that the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx is convergent, and its value is 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f (x) d x = \int_ {c _ {0}} ^ {c _ {1}} f (x) d x + \dots + \int_ {c _ {n - 1}} ^ {c _ {n}} f (x) d x.
$$

To justify this definition, we need to check that if $F ^ { \prime } \colon \alpha = d _ { 0 } < d _ { 1 } < \cdots < d _ { k - 1 } <$ $d _ { k } = \beta$ is another partition such that the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { d _ { i - 1 } } ^ { d _ { i } } f ( x )$ dx are convergent by Definition 19.1 or Definition 19.3, then 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \int_ {c _ {i - 1}} ^ {c _ {i}} f (x) d x = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {k} \int_ {d _ {j - 1}} ^ {d _ {j}} f (x) d x.\tag{19.6}
$$

Suppose first that we obtain the partition $F ^ { \prime }$ by adding one new base point to the partition $F \colon \alpha = c _ { 0 } < c _ { 1 } < \cdots < c _ { n - 1 } < c _ { n } = \beta$ . If this base point is $d \in \left( c _ { i - 1 } , c _ { i } \right)$ then to prove (19.6), we must show that 

$$
\int_ {c _ {i - 1}} ^ {c _ {i}} f (x) d x = \int_ {c _ {i - 1}} ^ {d} f (x) d x + \int_ {d} ^ {c _ {i}} f (x) d x.
$$

This is easy to check by distinguishing the cases appearing in Definitions 19.1 and 19.3, and using Theorem 14.38. 

Once we know this, we can use induction to find that (19.6) also holds if we obtain $F ^ { \prime }$ by adding any (finite) number of new base points. Finally, for the general case, consider the partition $F ^ { \prime \prime }$ , the union of the partitions $F$ and $F ^ { \prime }$ . By what we just said, both sides of (19.6) are equal to the sum of integrals corresponding to the partition $F ^ { \prime \prime }$ , so they are equal to each other. 

Examples 19.7. 1. The integral $\textstyle { \int _ { - \infty } ^ { \infty } d x } / ( 1 + x ^ { 2 } )$ is convergent, and its value is $\pi .$ Clearly, $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } d x / ( 1 + x ^ { 2 } ) = \pi / 2$ '<sub>and</sub> $\textstyle \int _ { - \infty } ^ { 0 } d x / ( 1 + x ^ { 2 } ) = \pi / 2$ by Example 19.5.5. 2. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { - 1 } ^ { 1 } d x / \left( { \sqrt { | x | } } \right)$ is convergent, and its value is 4. Clearly, $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } d x /$ $( { \sqrt { x } } ) = 2$ by Example 19.5.2. Similarly, we can show (or use the substitution $x = - t$ to reduce it to the previous integral) that $\textstyle \int _ { - 1 } ^ { 0 } d x / ( { \sqrt { - x } } ) = 2$ 

The methods used in Example 19.5 to compute improper integrals can be used in most cases in which the function we want to integrate has a primitive function: in such cases, the convergence of the improper integral depends on the existence of the limit of the primitive function. We introduce the following notation. Let $F$ be defined on the finite or infinite interval $( \alpha , \beta )$ . If the limits $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \alpha + 0 } F ( x )$ and $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \beta - 0 } F ( x )$ exist and are finite, then let 

$$
[ F ] _ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} = \lim _ {x \to \beta - 0} F (x) - \lim _ {x \to \alpha + 0} F (x).
$$

Here, when $\alpha = - \infty$ , the notation $\mathrm { l i m } _ { x  \alpha + 0 }$ means the limit at negative infinity, while if $\beta = \infty$ , then $\mathrm { l i m } _ { x  \beta - 0 }$ is the limit at positive infinity. 

Theorem 19.8. Let $f \colon ( \alpha , \beta )  \mathbb { R }$ be integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of $( \alpha , \beta )$ . Suppose that f has a primitive function in $( \alpha , \beta )$ , and let $F \colon ( \alpha , \beta )  \mathbb { R }$ be a primitive function of f. The improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx is convergent if and only if the finite limits $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \alpha + 0 } F ( x )$ and $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \beta - 0 } F ( x )$ exist, and then 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f (x) d x = [ F ] _ {\alpha} ^ {\beta}.
$$

Proof. Fix a point $x _ { 0 } \in ( \alpha , \beta )$ . Since f is integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval, it is easy to see that the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx is convergent if and only if the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { x _ { 0 } } f ( x )$ dx and $\textstyle \int _ { x _ { 0 } } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx are convergent by Definition 19.1 or 'Definition 19.3, and then 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f (x) d x = \int_ {\alpha} ^ {x _ {0}} f (x) d x + \int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {\beta} f (x) d x.
$$

By the fundamental theorem of calculus, 

$$
\int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {b} f (x) d x = F (b) - F (x _ {0})
$$

for all $x _ { 0 } < b < \beta$ . This implies that the limits $\mathrm { l i m } _ { b  \beta - 0 } [ F ( b ) - F ( x _ { 0 } ) ]$ along with $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { b \to \beta - 0 } \int _ { x _ { 0 } } ^ { b } f ( x ) } \end{array}$ dx either both exist or both do not exist, and if they do, then they 'agree. The same holds for the limits 

$$
\lim _ {a \to \alpha + 0} [ F (x _ {0}) - F (a) ] \quad \text { and } \quad \lim _ {a \to \alpha + 0} \int_ {a} ^ {x _ {0}} f (x)   d x
$$

as well. We get that the integral $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx is convergent if and only if the limits $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { b  \beta - 0 } [ F ( b ) - F ( x _ { 0 } ) ] } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { a  \alpha + 0 } [ F ( x _ { 0 } ) - F ( a ) ] } \end{array}$ exist and are finite, and then the value of the integral is the sum of these two limits. This is exactly what we wanted to show. □ 

We now turn to the rules of integration regarding improper integrals. We will see that the formulas for Riemann integration—including the rules for integration by parts and substitution—remain valid for improper integrals with almost no changes. 

Theorem 19.9. If the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } f d x$ and $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta }$ gdx are convergent, then the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } c \cdot f d x ( c \in \mathbb { R } )$ and $\textstyle { \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } ( f + g ) }$ dx are also convergent, and 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} c \cdot f d x = c \cdot \int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f d x \quad (c \in \mathbb {R})
$$

and 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} (f + g) d x = \int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f d x + \int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} g d x.
$$

Proof. The statement is clear by the definition of the improper integral, and by Theorems 14.30, 14.31, and 10.35. □ 

Theorem 19.10. Let the functions f and g be differentiable, and let f and $g ^ { \prime }$ be integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of $( \alpha , \beta )$ , and suppose that the limits $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \alpha + 0 } f g$ and $\mathrm { l i m } _ { x \to \beta - 0 } f g$ exist and arefinite. Then 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f ^ {\prime} g d x = [ f g ] _ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} - \int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f g ^ {\prime} d x,
$$

in the sense that ifone ofthe two improper integrals exists, then the other one does, too, and the two sides are equal. 

Proof. Fix a point $x _ { 0 } \in ( \alpha , \beta )$ . By Theorem 15.11, 

$$
\int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {b} f ^ {\prime} g d x = [ f g ] _ {x _ {0}} ^ {b} - \int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {b} f g ^ {\prime} d x
$$

for all $x _ { 0 } < b < \beta$ . Thus if we let b tend to $\beta - 0$ , then the left side has a limit if and only if the right side does, and if they exist, then they are equal. Similarly, if $a  \alpha + 0$ , then the left side of the equality 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {x _ {0}} f ^ {\prime} g d x = [ f g ] _ {a} ^ {x _ {0}} - \int_ {a} ^ {x _ {0}} f g ^ {\prime} d x
$$

has a limit if and only if the right side does, and if they exist, then they are equal. We can now get the statement of the theorem just as in the proof of Theorem 19.8. 

We defined Riemann integrals $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d x$ for the case $b \leq a$ (see Definition 14.40) 'We should make this generalization for improper integrals as well. 

Definition 19.11. If the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx exists, then let 

$$
\int_ {\beta} ^ {\alpha} f (x) d x = - \int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f (x) d x.
$$

The value of the integral $\textstyle \int _ { \alpha } ^ { \alpha } f d x$ is zero for all $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ and $\alpha = \pm \infty$ , and for every function $f$ '(whether it is defined at the point α or not). 

Theorem 19.12. Let $( \alpha , \beta )$ be a finite or infinite open interval. Let g be strictly monotone and differentiable, and suppose that $g ^ { \prime }$ is integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of $( \alpha , \beta ) . L e t ^ { 1 } \mathrm { l i m } _ { x  \alpha + 0 } g ( x ) = \gamma a n d \mathrm { l i m } _ { x  \beta - 0 } g ( x ) = \delta . I f f$ is continuous on the open interval $( \gamma , \delta )$ , then 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {\beta} f (g (t)) \cdot g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = \int_ {\gamma} ^ {\delta} f (x) d x\tag{19.7}
$$

in the sense that if one of the two improper integrals is convergent, then so is the other, and they are equal. 

Proof. We suppose that $g$ is strictly monotone increasing (we can argue similarly if $g$ is monotone decreasing). Then $\gamma < \delta$ . Fix a number $x _ { 0 } \in ( \alpha , \beta )$ , and let $\textstyle F ( x ) = \int _ { x _ { 0 } } ^ { x } f ( t )$ dt for all $x \in ( \gamma , \delta )$ . By the definition of the improper integral, it 'follows that the right-hand side of (19.7) is convergent if and only if the finite limits $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \gamma + 0 } F ( x )$ and $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \delta - 0 } F ( x )$ exist, and then the value of the integral on the right-hand side of (19.7) is $\left[ F \right] _ { \gamma } ^ { \delta }$ 

By Theorem 15.5, F is a primitive function of f on the interval $( \gamma , \delta )$ , and so by the differentiation rule for compositions of functions, $F \circ g$ is a primitive function of $( f \circ g ) \cdot g ^ { \prime }$ on $( \alpha , \beta )$ . By Theorem 19.8, the left-hand side of $( 1 9 . 7 )$ is convergent if and only if the finite limits $\textstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t \to \alpha + 0 } F { \bigl ( } g ( t ) { \bigr ) }$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \beta - 0 } F ( g ( t ) ) } \end{array}$ ) exist, and then the value of the integral on the left-end side of (19.7) is $[ F \circ g ] _ { \alpha } ^ { \beta } .$ 

Now if $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x  \gamma + 0 } F ( x ) = A . } \end{array}$ , then by Theorem 10.41 on the limit of compositions of functions, $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \alpha + 0 } F ( g ( t ) ) = A . } \end{array}$ . Conversely, if $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \alpha + 0 } F ( g ( t ) ) = A } \end{array}$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x  \gamma + 0 } F ( x ) = A ; } \end{array}$ ; clearly, the function $g ^ { - 1 }$ maps the interval $( \gamma , \delta )$ onto the interval $( \alpha , \beta )$ in a strictly monotone increasing way, and so $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \gamma + 0 } g ^ { - 1 } ( x ) = \alpha } \end{array}$ . Thus if $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { t  \alpha + 0 } F ( g ( t ) ) = A } \end{array}$ , then $\textstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \gamma + 0 } F ( x ) = A$ , since $F = ( F \circ g ) \circ g ^ { - 1 }$ 

The same reasoning gives that the limit $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \delta - 0 } F ( x )$ exists if and only if $\mathrm { l i m } _ { t  \beta - 0 } F ( g ( t ) )$ exists, and then they are equal. 

Comparing all of the results above, we get the statement of the theorem we set out to prove. □ 

The theorem above is true with much weaker conditions as well: it is not necessary to require the monotonicity of $g$ (at least if $\gamma \neq \delta )$ , and instead of the continuity of $f ,$ , it suffices to assume that $f$ is integrable in the closed and bounded subintervals of the image of $g .$ . The precise theorem is as follows. 

Theorem 19.13. Let $g$ be differentiable, suppose $g ^ { \prime }$ is integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of $( \alpha , \beta )$ , and suppose that the finite or infinite limits $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \alpha + 0 } g ( x ) = \gamma } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \beta - 0 } g ( x ) = \delta } \end{array}$ exist. Let f be integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval ofthe image ofg, that is, of $g ( ( \alpha , \beta ) )$ ). 

(i) $I f \gamma \neq \delta$ , then (19.7) holds in the sense that ifone ofthe two improper integrals exists, then so does the other, and then they are equal. 

(ii) $I f \gamma = \delta$ and the left-hand side of (19.7) is convergent, then its value is zero. 

We give the proof of the theorem in the appendix of the chapter. We note that when $\gamma = \delta$ , the left-hand side of (19.7) is not necessarily convergent; see Exercise 19.12. 

Remark 19.14. We have seen examples in which we created improper integrals from “ordinary” Riemann integrals. The reverse case can occur as well: we can create a Riemann integral starting from an improper integral. For example, the substitution x = sint gives us 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} \frac {x ^ {n}}{\sqrt {1 - x ^ {2}}} d x = \int_ {0} ^ {\frac {\pi}{2}} \sin^ {n} t d t,
$$

and the substitution $x = 1 / t$ gives us 

$$
\int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {d x}{1 + x ^ {2}} = \int_ {1} ^ {0} \frac {1}{1 + 1 / t ^ {2}} \cdot \frac {- 1}{t ^ {2}} d t = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \frac {d t}{1 + t ^ {2}} = \frac {\pi}{4}.
$$

## 19.2 The Convergence of Improper Integrals

In the applications of improper integrals, the most important question is whether a given integral is convergent; computing the value of the integral if it is convergent is often only a secondary (or hopeless) task. Suppose that $f$ is integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of the interval $[ a , \beta )$ . The convergence of the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f d x$ depends only on the values of $f$ close to $\beta \mathrm { : }$ : for every $a < b < \beta$ , the integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f$ dx is convergent if and only if the integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { b } ^ { \beta } f d x } \end{array}$ is convergent. Clearly, 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {\omega} f d x = \int_ {a} ^ {b} f d x + \int_ {b} ^ {\omega} f d x
$$

for all $b < \omega < \beta$ , so if $\omega  \beta - 0$ , then the left-hand side has a finite limit if and only if the same holds for $\textstyle \int _ { b } ^ { \omega } f d x$ 

From Examples 19.2 and 19.5, we might want to conclude that an integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { b } ^ { \beta } f d x } \end{array}$ can be convergent only if $f$ tends to zero fast enough as $x  \beta - 0$ '. However, this is not the case. Consider a convergent integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { b } ^ { \beta } f d x } \end{array}$ (for example, any of the 'convergent integrals appearing in the examples above), and change the values of $f$ arbitrarily at the points of a sequence $x _ { n }  \beta - 0$ . This does not affect the convergence of the integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f d x . } \end{array}$ , since for all $a < b < \beta$ , the value of the function $f$ is 'changed at only finitely many points inside the interval $[ a , b ]$ , so the Riemann integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { b } f d x$ does not change either. On the other hand, if at the point $x _ { n }$ we give $f$ 'the value n for every $n ,$ , then this new function does not tend to $_ 0$ at $\beta$ . In fact we can find continuous functions $f$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { b } ^ { \beta } f d x } \end{array}$ is convergent but $f$ does not tend to 0 at $\beta$ (see Exercises 19.28 and 19.29). 

The converse of the (false) statement above, however, is true: if $f$ tends to zero fast enough as $x \to \beta - 0$ , then the integral $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { b } ^ { \beta } f d x } \end{array}$ is convergent. To help with the 'proof of this, we first give a necessary and sufficient condition for the convergence of integrals, which we call Cauchy’s criterion for improper integrals. 

Theorem 19.15 (Cauchy’s Criterion). Let f be integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of the interval $[ a , \beta )$ . The improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \tilde { \beta } }$ fdx is convergent if and only iffor every $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a number $a \leq b < \beta$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \left| \int _ { b _ { 1 } } ^ { b _ { 2 } } f ( x ) d x \right| < \varepsilon } \end{array}$ for all $b < b _ { 1 } < b _ { 2 } < \beta$ 

 Proof. The statement follows simply from Cauchy’s criterion for limits of functions (Theorem 10.34) and the equality 

$$
\int_ {a} ^ {b _ {2}} f (x) d x - \int_ {a} ^ {b _ {1}} f (x) d x = \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} f (x) d x.
$$

Suppose that $f$ is integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of the interval $[ a , \beta )$ . If $f$ is nonnegative on $[ a , \beta )$ , then the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f d x$ always exists. This is because the function $\begin{array} { r } { \omega \mapsto \int _ { a } ^ { \omega } f d x \left( \omega \in [ a , \beta ) \right) } \end{array}$ 'is monotone increasing, and so the finite or infinite limit lim $\begin{array} { r } { { ^ { \mathrm { l } } \omega \mathrm {  } \beta \mathrm { - } 0 \int _ { a } ^ { \omega } f d x } } \end{array}$ must necessarily exist by Theorem 10.68. 

Thus if $f$ is integrable on every closed and bounded subinterval of the interval $[ a , \beta )$ , then the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } | f |$ dx exists for sure. The question is whether its value is finite. 

Definition 19.16. We call the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f d x$ absolutely convergent if f is 'integrable on the closed and bounded subintervals of $[ a , \beta )$ and the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } | f | d x$ is convergent. 

Theorem 19.17. Ifthe improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f$ dx is absolutely convergent, then it is convergent. 

Proof. The statement clearly follows from Cauchy’s criterion, since 

$$
\left| \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} f (x) d x \right| \leq \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} | f (x) | d x
$$

for all $a \leq b _ { 1 } < b _ { 2 } < \beta$ 

The converse of the statement is generally not true; we will soon see in Examples 19.20.3 and 19.20.4 that the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } ( \sin x / x )$ dx is convergent but not absolutely convergent. 

The following theorem—which is one of the most often used criteria for convergence—is called the majorization principle. 

Theorem 19.18 (Majorization Principle). Let f and g be integrable in every closed and bounded subinterval of $[ a , \beta )$ , and suppose that there exists a $b _ { 0 } \in [ a , \beta )$ such that $| f ( x ) | \leq g ( x )$ for all $x \in \mathit { \Gamma } \left( b _ { 0 } , \beta \right)$ . If $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } g ( x )$ dx is convergent, then so is $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx. 

Proof. By the “only $\mathrm { i f } ^ { \dag }$ part of Theorem 19.15, if $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } g ( x )$ dx is convergent, then for an arbitrary $\varepsilon > 0$ , there exists a $b < \beta$ such that 

$$
\left| \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} g (x) d x \right| <   \varepsilon
$$

holds for all $b < b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } < \beta$ . Since $| f ( x ) | \leq g ( x )$ in the interval $( b _ { 0 } , \beta )$ 

$$
\left| \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} f (x) d x \right| \leq \left| \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} | f (x) | d x \right| \leq \left| \int_ {b _ {1}} ^ {b _ {2}} g (x) d x \right| <   \varepsilon
$$

for all max $( b , b _ { 0 } ) < b _ { 1 } , b _ { 2 } < \beta$ . Thus by the $\ " _ { 1 1 } \cdot \overrightarrow { }$ part of Theorem 19.15, the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx is convergent. □ 

Remark $I 9 . I 9 .$ . The majorization principle can be used to show divergence as well: if $g ( x ) \geq | f ( x ) |$ for all $x \in ( b _ { 0 } , \beta )$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f ( x ) } \end{array}$ dx is divergent, then it follows that $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } g ( x )$ dx is also divergent. Clearly, if this latter integral were convergent, then $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \beta } f ( x )$ dx would be convergent as well. 

Such applications of the theorem are often called minorization. 

Examples 19.20. 1. The integrals $\scriptstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } ( \sin x / x ^ { 2 } )$ dx and $\scriptstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } ( \cos x / x ^ { 2 } )$ dx are convergent, since $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } x ^ { - 2 }$ 'dx is convergent, and 

$$
\left| \frac {\sin x}{x ^ {2}} \right| \leq \frac {1}{x ^ {2}} \quad \text { and } \quad \left| \frac {\cos x}{x ^ {2}} \right| \leq \frac {1}{x ^ {2}}
$$

for all $x \geq 1$ 

2. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } ( \sin x / x ^ { 2 } )$ dx is divergent. We know that $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to 0 } \sin x / x = 1$ , so sin $x / x > 1 / 2$ if $0 < x < \delta _ { 0 }$ , and so sin $\hat { x / x ^ { 2 } } > 1 / x \mathrm { i f } 0 < x < \delta _ { 0 }$ . Thus by the divergence of $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \delta _ { 0 } } x ^ { - 1 } d x$ , it follows that $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } ( \sin x / x ^ { 2 } )$ dx is divergent. 

'3. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } ( \sin x / x )$ 'dx is convergent. 

'We can easily show this with the help of integration by parts. Since 

$$
\int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {\sin x}{x} d x = \left[ - \frac {1}{x} \cdot \cos x \right] _ {1} ^ {\omega} - \int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {\cos x}{x ^ {2}} d x
$$

for all $\omega > 1$ 

$$
\int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {\sin x}{x} d x = \cos 1 - \int_ {1} ^ {\infty} \frac {\cos x}{x ^ {2}} d x.
$$

4. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } | \sin x / x |$ dx is divergent. Since $| \sin x | \geq \sin ^ { 2 } x$ for all x, to show 'that the integral is divergent it suffices to show that $\scriptstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } ( \sin ^ { 2 } x / x )$ dx is divergent. We 

know that 

$$
\int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {\sin^ {2} x}{x} d x = \frac {1}{2} \cdot \int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {1 - \cos 2 x}{x} d x = \frac {1}{2} \cdot \int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {d x}{x} - \frac {1}{2} \cdot \int_ {1} ^ {\omega} \frac {\cos 2 x}{x} d x.
$$

Similarly to Example 3, we can show that if $\omega  \infty$ , then the second term on the right-hand side is convergent, while $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 1 } ^ { \omega } d x / x \to \infty \mathrm { a s } \omega \to \infty } \end{array}$ . Thus $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } \sin ^ { 2 } x /$ $x d x = \infty$ 

5. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } } d x$ is convergent, and in fact, $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } x ^ { c } e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } } d x$ is also convergent for all $c > 0$ . Clearly, $e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } } < 1 / | x | ^ { c + 2 } \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } | x | > x _ { 0 } , \mathrm { ~ s o ~ } | x ^ { c } e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } } | < 1 / x ^ { 2 } \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } | x | > x _ { 0 } .$ 

Example 19.21. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } x ^ { c } \cdot e ^ { - x } d x$ is convergent if $c > - 1$ 

Let us inspect the integrals $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 }$ and $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty }$ separately. The integral $\textstyle \int _ { 1 } ^ { \infty } x ^ { c } \ e ^ { - x } d x$ is convergent for all $c \mathrm { : }$ ' ' 'we can prove this in the same way as in Example $1 9 . 2 0 . 5$ 

$c \geq 0$ , then $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } x ^ { c } \cdot e ^ { - x } d x$ is an ordinary integral. $\mathrm { I f } - 1 < c < 0 .$ , then we can 'apply the majorization principle: since if $x \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ , then $| x ^ { c } \cdot e ^ { - x } | \leq x ^ { c }$ and the integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } x ^ { c } d x$ is convergent, we know that the integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } x ^ { c } \cdot e ^ { - x } d x$ is also convergent. 

The integral appearing in the example above (as a function of c) appears in applications so often that it gets its own notation. Leonhard Euler, who first worked with this integral, found it more useful to define this function on the interval $( 0 , \infty )$ instead of $( - 1 , \infty )$ , so instead of notation for the integral in Example 19.21, he introduced it for the integral $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } x ^ { c - 1 } \cdot e ^ { - x } d x$ , and this is still used today. 

We use $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( \boldsymbol { c } )$ to denote the value of the integral $\textstyle { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } x ^ { c - 1 } \cdot e ^ { - x } d x }$ for all $c > 0$ 

So for example, $\begin{array} { r } { T ( 1 ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty } e ^ { - x } d x = 1 } \end{array}$ 

One can show that $\boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( \boldsymbol { c } + 1 ) = \boldsymbol { c } \cdot \boldsymbol { \Gamma } ( \boldsymbol { c } )$ for all $c > 0$ . Once we know this, it easily follows that $\Gamma ( n ) = ( n - 1 ) !$ for every positive integer n (see Exercises 19.38 and 19.39). It is known that $\varGamma$ is not an elementary function. To see more properties of the function Γ, see Exercises 19.41–19.46. 

Example 19.20.3 can be greatly generalized. The following theorem gives us a convergence criterion according to which we could replace $1 / x$ in the example by any monotone function that tends to zero at infinity, and we could replace sinx by any function whose integral function is bounded. 

Theorem 19.22. Suppose that 

(i) the function f is monotone on the interval $[ a , \infty )$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x  \infty } f ( x ) = 0 } \end{array}$ , and moreover, 

(ii) the function g is integrable on $[ a , b ]$ for all $b > a ,$ , and the integral function $\begin{array} { r } { G ( x ) = \int _ { a } ^ { x } g ( t ) } \end{array}$ dt is bounded on $[ a , \infty )$ 

Then the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \infty } f ( x ) g ( x )$ dx is convergent. 

Proof. Suppose that $\begin{array} { r } { | \int _ { a } ^ { x } g ( t ) d t | \le K } \end{array}$ for all $x \geq a$ . Then $\textstyle | \int _ { x } ^ { y } g ( t ) d t | \leq 2 K$ for all $a \leq x < y$ , since $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { x } ^ { y } g ( \bar { t } ) d t = \int _ { a } ^ { y } g ( t ) d t - \int _ { a } ^ { y } g ( t ) d t } \end{array}$ . Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be given. Since $\scriptstyle \operatorname* { l i m } _ { x \to \infty } f ( x ) = 0$ ', there exists an $x _ { 0 }$ such that $| f ( x ) | < \varepsilon$ for all $x \geq x _ { 0 } . \operatorname { I f } x _ { 0 } \leq x < y$ then by the second mean value theorem of integration (Theorem 15.8), we get that for a suitable $\xi \in [ x , y ]$ ， 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \left| \int_ {x} ^ {y} f (t) g (t) d t \right| \leq | f (x) | \cdot \left| \int_ {x} ^ {\xi} g (t) d t \right| + | f (y) | \cdot \left| \int_ {\xi} ^ {y} g (t) d t \right| \leq \\ \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \qquad \leq \varepsilon \cdot 2 K + \varepsilon \cdot 2 K = 4 K \varepsilon . \end{array}
$$

Since ε was arbitrary, we have shown that the improper integral $\textstyle \int _ { a } ^ { \infty } f ( x ) g ( x )$ dx satisfies Cauchy’s criterion, so it is convergent. □

## 19.3 Appendix: Proof of Theorem 19.13

Fix a point $x _ { 0 } \in ( \alpha , \beta )$ . We first show that 

$$
\int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {\beta} f (g (t)) \cdot g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = \int_ {g (x _ {0})} ^ {\delta} f (x) d x,\tag{19.10}
$$

in the sense that if one of the two improper integrals is convergent, then so is the other, and they are equal. We distinguish two cases. 

I. First we suppose that the value $\delta$ is finite, and that g takes on the value $\delta$ in the interval $[ x _ { 0 } , \beta )$ . Let $\left( c _ { n } \right)$ be a sequence such that $c _ { n }  \beta$ and $c _ { n } < \beta$ for all n. Then $g ( c _ { n } )  \delta$ , and so it easily follows that the set H consisting of the numbers $g ( x _ { 0 } )$ $\delta .$ , and $g ( c _ { n } ) ( n = 1 , 2 , . . . )$ has a greatest and a smallest element. (This is because if there is an element greater than max $( g ( x _ { 0 } ) , \delta )$ in H, namely some $g ( c _ { n } )$ , then there can be only finitely many elements greater than this, so there will be a greatest among these. This proves that H has a greatest element. We can argue similarly to show that H has a smallest element, too.) If $m = \operatorname* { m i n } H$ and $M = \operatorname* { m a x } H$ , then by the continuity of $g _ { \mathrm { : } }$ we know that $[ m , M ]$ is a closed and bounded subinterval of the image of the function g. By the condition, $f$ is integrable on $[ m , M ]$ . Thus $f$ is also integrable on the interval $[ g ( x _ { 0 } ) , \delta ]$ by Theorem 14.37. Let $\textstyle \int _ { g ( x _ { 0 } ) } ^ { \delta } f ( x ) d x = I .$ . Since the integral function of $f$ is continuous on $[ m , M ]$ by Theorem 15.5, 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {g (x _ {0})} ^ {g (c _ {n})} f (x) d x = I.\tag{19.11}
$$

Now applying the substitution formula (that is, Theorem 15.22) with the interval $[ x _ { 0 } , c _ { n } ]$ , we obtain 

$$
\int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {c _ {n}} f (g (t)) \cdot g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = \int_ {g (x _ {0})} ^ {g (c _ {n})} f (x) d x\tag{19.12}
$$

for all $n ,$ which we can combine with (19.11) to find that 

$$
\lim _ {n \rightarrow \infty} \int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {c _ {n}} f (g (t)) \cdot g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = I.\tag{19.13}
$$

Since this holds for every sequence $c _ { n }  \beta , c _ { n } < \beta$ , 

$$
\lim _ {c \rightarrow \beta} \int_ {x _ {0}} ^ {c} f (g (t)) \cdot g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = I,\tag{19.14}
$$

which—by the definition of the improper integral—means that the integral on the left-hand side of (19.10) is convergent, and its value is I. 

II. Now suppose that g does not take on the value $\delta$ in the interval $[ x _ { 0 } , \beta )$ (including the case $\delta = \infty \ \mathrm { o r } \ \delta = - \infty )$ . Since $g$ is continuous, the Bolzano–Darboux theorem implies that either $g ( x ) < \delta$ for all $x \in [ x _ { 0 } , \beta )$ (this includes the case $\delta = \infty )$ , or $g ( x ) > \delta$ for all $x \in [ x _ { 0 } , \beta )$ (this includes the case $\delta = - \infty )$ . We can assume that the first case holds (since the second one can be treated in the same way). Then $[ g ( x _ { 0 } ) , \delta ) \subset g ( [ x _ { 0 } , \beta ) )$ . 

Suppose that the right-hand side of (19.10) is convergent, and that its value is I. If $c _ { n }  \beta$ and $c _ { n } < \beta$ for all n, then $g ( c _ { n } )  \delta$ and $g ( c _ { n } ) < \delta$ for all n. Thus (19.11) and (19.12) give us (19.13) once again. Since this holds for every sequence $c _ { n }  \beta$ $c _ { n } < \beta$ , we also know that (19.14) holds, that is, the integral on the left-hand side of (19.10) is convergent, and its value is I. 

Now finally, let us suppose that the left-hand side of (19.10) is convergent and that its value is I. Let $\left( d _ { n } \right)$ be a sequence such that $d _ { n } \to \delta$ and $g ( x _ { 0 } ) \leq d _ { n } < \delta$ for all n. Since $[ g ( x _ { 0 } ) , \delta ) \subset g ( [ x _ { 0 } , \beta ) )$ , there exist points $c _ { n } \in [ x _ { 0 } , \beta )$ such that $d _ { n } = g ( c _ { n } )$ $( n = 1 , 2 , \ldots )$ . We now show that $c _ { n }  \beta$ . Since $c _ { n } < \beta$ for all $n ,$ , it suffices to show that for all $b < \beta$ , we have $c _ { n } > b$ if n is sufficiently large. 

We can assume that $x _ { 0 } \leq b < \beta$ . Since g is continuous, it must have a maximum value in $[ x _ { 0 } , b ]$ . If this is $A ,$ , then $A < \delta$ , since we assumed every value of $g$ to be smaller than δ. By the condition $d _ { n } \to \delta$ , we know that $d _ { n } > A$ if $n > n _ { 0 }$ . Since $d _ { n } = g ( c _ { n } )$ , if $n > n _ { 0 }$ , then $c _ { n } > b ,$ , since $c _ { n } \leq b$ would imply that $g ( c _ { n } ) \leq A$ 

This shows that $c _ { n }  \beta$ . This, in turn, implies that the left-hand side of (19.12) tends to I as $n \to \infty$ . Since the right-hand side of (19.12) is $\textstyle \int _ { g ( x _ { 0 } ) } ^ { d _ { n } } f ( x ) d x$ , we have shown that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} \int_ {g (x _ {0})} ^ {d _ {n}} f (x) d x = I.
$$

This holds for every sequence $d _ { n } \to \delta , \ d _ { n } < \delta$ , so the integral on the right-hand side of (19.10) is convergent, and its value is I. This proves (19.10). The exact same argument shows that 

$$
\int_ {\alpha} ^ {x _ {0}} f (g (t)) \cdot g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = \int_ {\gamma} ^ {g (x _ {0})} f (x) d x\tag{19.15}
$$

in the sense that if one of the two improper integrals exists, then so does the other, and they are equal. 

Now we turn to the proof of the theorem. Suppose that $\gamma \neq \delta$ . We can assume that $\gamma < \delta$ , since the case $\gamma > \delta$ is similar. Then the interval $( \gamma , \delta )$ ) is part of the image of $g ,$ so there exists a point $x _ { 0 } \in ( \alpha , \beta )$ such that $g ( x _ { 0 } ) \in ( \gamma , \delta )$ . By the definition of the improper integral, it follows that the left-hand side of (19.7) is convergent if and only if the left-hand sides of (19.10) and (19.15) are convergent, and then it is equal to their sum. The same holds for the right-hand sides. Thus (19.10) and (19.15) immediately prove statement (i) of the theorem. 

Now suppose that $\gamma = \delta$ and that the left-hand side of (19.7) is convergent. Then the left-hand sides of (19.10) and (19.15) are also convergent. Thus the corresponding right-hand sides are also convergent, and (19.10) and (19.15) both hold. Since the sum of the right-hand sides of (19.10) and (19.15) is $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \gamma } ^ { \delta } f d x = 0 } \end{array}$ , the left-hand side of (19.7) is also zero.

2.3 Let ${ \mathcal { H } } _ { n }$ denote the system of sets $H \subset \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ satisfying the condition, and let $a _ { n }$ be the number of elements in ${ \mathcal { H } } _ { n }$ . It is easy to check that $a _ { 1 } = 2$ and $a _ { 2 } = 3$ (the empty set works, too). If $n > 2$ , then we can show that for every $H \subset \{ 1 , \ldots , n \}$ 

$$
\begin{array}{c} H \in \mathcal {H} _ {n} \iff [ (n \notin H) \land (H \cap \{1, \ldots , n - 1 \} \in \mathcal {H} _ {n - 1}) ] \lor \\ \lor [ (n \in H) \land (H \cap \{1, \ldots , n - 2 \} \in \mathcal {H} _ {n - 2}) \land (n - 1 \notin H) ]. \end{array}
$$

It is then clear that for $n > 2$ , we have $a _ { n } = a _ { n - 1 } + a _ { n - 2 }$ . Thus the sequence of numbers $a _ { n }$ is $2 , 3 , 5 , 8 , \ldots$ . This is called the Fibonacci sequence, which has an explicit formula (see Exercise 4.3).

$$
\sqrt [ n ]{1 + n a} \leq ((1 + n a) + n - 1) / n = 1 + a.
$$

If we raise both sides to the nth power, then we get the inequality we want to prove.
